rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of unobserved late compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster and late doublet. The short elution window leaves ample room to use a shallower gradient afterward if needed.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map temperature-dependent selectivity before optimizing slope. This may separate the nearly coincident middle peaks differently from the two warmer runs.
The 25 C run gives the best selectivity, with only two pairs below target. A shallower gradient should improve their separation while using the available margin before the 10-minute time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction while retaining the 18-minute gradient, making the slope shallower without extending the elution window. This tests whether the remaining critical pair can reach R ≥ 1.5 while the last peak stays below 10 minutes.
Use the time margin gained by starting at 0.20 organic to lengthen the gradient and improve the remaining critical pair. The last peak is expected to remain near, but below, 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a one-step shorter gradient to reduce elution time while retaining full resolution. This brackets the critical-pair threshold between the 18- and 22-minute gradients.

Return to the successful 22-minute duration and raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention. This tests whether its resolution margin can accommodate a faster elution window while preserving CRF 1.000.
Test a one-step temperature increase from the fully resolved method to shorten retention and measure its effect on the critical pair. Keep injection 6 as the established maximum-score fallback.

At the higher starting organic fraction, lengthen the gradient to recover critical-pair resolution while retaining the earlier elution window. This could produce full resolution slightly faster than injection 6; the temperature returns to the more favorable 25 C.
Shorten the latest fully resolved gradient by one grid step to locate the fastest acceptable setting at phi0 0.25. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower slope to offset the loss of critical-pair selectivity. This explores whether the early portion of the gradient can be removed while retaining full resolution and a last peak below 9 minutes.

Explore a faster selectivity regime: the middle pair changed elution order between the 10- and 18-minute gradients at 25 C, suggesting a steeper gradient could separate it again. A modest temperature increase may also improve the late pair; the maximum-score methods remain established fallbacks.

Lower temperature while holding the fast gradient fixed to test whether the crowded middle cluster opens up. Comparing this run with injections 3 and 13 will show whether the fast-gradient regime can support a shorter fully resolved method.

Test a modest temperature increase on the faster fully resolved method. Its larger separation before the middle doublet may tolerate the temperature-induced selectivity shift better than injection 9, potentially preserving full resolution with earlier elution.

Probe beyond the temperature-dependent late-pair crossing to see whether separation recovers at a shorter retention time. The middle cluster may also change order, so this tests a new selectivity regime rather than assuming uniform improvement with temperature.

Test the high-temperature endpoint with this shallow gradient to seek a faster fully resolved selectivity regime. The earlier 60 C run used a much steeper gradient, so its unresolved pairs do not rule out success here.

Test 45 C to move away from the close middle pair seen at 40 C without reaching the crowded high-temperature pattern. This intermediate temperature may provide full resolution with a substantially shorter elution window than the confirmed 25 C methods.
Make the 45 C gradient shallower to improve the three moderately unresolved pairs. The current last peak at 6.72 minutes leaves substantial room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

Test the remaining temperature step between 30 and 40 C near the best shallow-gradient method. This may move the late doublet away from its crossing while retaining adequate middle-cluster selectivity; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Lower the starting organic fraction at 45 C to alter selectivity in the middle cluster and late doublet rather than simply flattening the gradient further. The short retention window leaves room for this adjustment, while the confirmed CRF 1.000 methods remain available.

Refine the established maximum-score region with a slope between injections 6 and 7, using the endpoint grid for a smaller slope adjustment. This should approach the critical-pair resolution threshold while potentially eluting the last peak slightly earlier than injection 10.

Test a lower starting fraction with a steeper gradient to seek another fully resolved method near the nine-minute boundary. This probes the untested starting-fraction step between 0.10 and 0.20 while retaining injection 22 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 22 using a narrower gradient window, aiming to shave retention time while keeping the critical pair at R ≥ 1.5. This is a fine adjustment near the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Back off to a slightly shallower slope than injection 24 to restore full resolution, while narrowing the endpoint to shorten the programmed gradient. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, before the gradient ends, targeting CRF 1.000.
